utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, would you have the accused brought in, please. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are the interpreters ready? All our interpreter friends are ready. Does everybody hear? Good morning, everybody. Does everybody hear? Does the Prosecutor hear, Mr. Blaskic, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLASKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour, I can hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would first like to ask the Registrar if we might move into a private session. We are now going to use the expression "huit clos partiel" instead of "session privée‚". (In private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would just note, your Honour, we do not have a reason to object to protective measures, but we have not been told who this witness is or what protective measures are being requested. There may be instances where we would have an objection and I think it would speed the procedure if generally we were told before the witness comes what is going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that objection by Mr. Hayman is relevant. There has been that decision taken, there has been a list, but one should indicate protected witness and what those protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we have done that routinely, as counsel knows. This particular protected witness, and I will gladly tell counsel who that is and the court, if we go into private session, but the protection requested is full body, voice and pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Registrar, these protective measures, they have been taken pursuant to an order, could you refresh my memory?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, I do not think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So we have to be careful here. In our order, our decision from January or February I believe, we have taken general measures, obliging the Defence to do similar things, I think, to abide by the proper form. Just one second. Before bringing in the witness, generally speaking the court must protect witnesses but Prosecutor, I do think that we sort out these measures via the Registrar. It would be important because the Defence sometimes would like to enter into a discussion on these points. That is all I have to say now, we can bring in the witness. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness J, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now we are going to have you take your solemn oath which all witnesses must make, it is an oath, so the Registrar is going to provide you this. We are going to deal with you as an anonymous witness but we do have to make sure that you are the witness called by the Prosecution. The Registrar --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please remain seated and read out the oath. WITNESS J (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness J, you have accepted at the request of the Prosecution -- can you hear me, madam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have accepted to testify about events you saw. The Tribunal is going to ask you about these events at a given point in time when the Prosecution believes it is appropriate, or when fellow judges believe it is appropriate. You will have questions put to you to refocus, as it were, your testimony on the essential events, and then as the Prosecutor probably told you, when you are done with your testimony, of course, the counsel of the accused, because we are in a court of law, will be putting questions to you as well. Obviously all this will take place under the control of the judges. Please relax, there is nothing to be afraid of, and we will try to be brief, but at the same time do take your time. You certainly came because you witnessed the events on 16th April 1993, events that affected you personally and your property, your family, and you are going to tell us with your words, as you see fit. And you had dealings with military units, you tell us about that, and then, of course, the Prosecutor will be able to interrupt you, but simply to keep you on the straight and narrow path, because there is no point going into everything. What the Prosecutor wants you to say is what we really want to hear. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So by your leave, will you please tell us what you want to tell us about these events on 16th April. Please, go right ahead and from time to time the Prosecutor will redirect the tack you have taken as and when necessary. We are listening to you, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 15th May 1992, I had to leave Karaula because of the aggression. I left with my children who were small. I moved to Vitez where I lived until 28th December 1992. After that, I moved to Ahmici. That is where we stayed until 16th April, until the attack. Until then, everything was normal, we did not have any problems. That night, we also went to bed to go to sleep and in the morning, early, I heard (inaudible) first bullets hit the windows of the house where I was living. My child, my mother and my brother's wife were sleeping in one room, and then the incendiary bullets hit the bedding and then I was sleeping in the other room with my husband and my youngest child, the shooting continued. We did not know what to do. We hid behind the furniture. We did not stay there very long. After that, we heard a burst of fire into the door. After the burst of fire, some soldiers walked in. I did not see them. I only heard their voices, and they said, "come out. If we find you, you will fare worse". We remained seated. They came to the door that was ajar, and in the same voice, they repeated, "come out. If we find you, you will fare worse". I tried to come out, my husband forbid me, he said, "stay with the children, I am going to go, you are the mother, you have to be with them". He got up and walked towards the door. He held his hands up and he only told them, "people, do not shoot, I have small children here in the room". They did not say anything to him, they just shot at him. I did not hear a big explosion or anything, a loud noise. I think there was a silencer there or something. I could only see my husband falling down by the door. I did not see a big wound on the stomach, but when I tried to pull him into the room, I noticed on the back that his intestines were all spilled outside. They returned the moment they shot him and I only heard them, "we can go, the Joe is done in here". My children were screaming and yelling, "daddy". We thought we could help him, but it was too late.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted), "is anybody alive? You have to move, your house is on fire. It was hit by a shell". We were unprepared, still in pyjamas. She helped us put some clothes on the children and we started for the door. My daughter, who was only 5 years old, was crying and she said she would not leave daddy to burn there but we could not pull him out, we did not even know what to do with ourselves. They all went in the direction of the house of Vlado Santic, who was across from a field. My child did not want to leave the house, she was crying and me too, how could we leave the body to burn, but we had to leave because the roof was already caving in. I summoned some strength and I started running across the field. When I came about halfway across the field, there was some shooting, something powerful. I could only sense that I was -- big chunks of earth fell on me and then I fell down together with my child. When I felt that the shooting was subsiding, I got up and moved on. We arrived in front of Vlado's house, that is where we were looking for some kind of a rescue, all the Muslim houses were already on fire. We tried to enter, it was locked. My neighbour called out, but nobody responded. The other structures around his house were also padlocked and we could not enter anywhere. There was only one shed which was open and that is where we entered. We sat there, we could still hear the shooting, but no bullet ever hit that house or that shed. So we saw that we were safe there, and after sitting there -- after we sat there for a while, the first group of soldiers arrived and they were calling Vlado by the name, they were banging at the door. He did not respond. One of them said, "do not ring the bell, you know that he has already left with his family". They did not look towards the shed, they did not notice us, but I did notice that they were painted with black paint on their face, they had rifles and camouflage uniforms and on the arm, they had a patch with the HVO, with the chequer-board. They left and then we stayed. My children were crying, they said they were hungry, I had nothing to give them. My neighbour tried to get in through the window so that she could bring something out of Vlado's house, but she could not because of the shooting, so we stayed there, sitting down and my children said, "mum, bring us something from our own house", but by that time, our own house had already burnt down. After a while, the second group of soldiers arrived, also in camouflage uniforms with the HVO insignia. They did not have their faces painted. They had rifles. They had white belts, they had bandoleers and they had knives at their belts. They were asking why this house was not on fire, one of them said, "it is a Croatian house, that is why it is not in flames". As they were saying this, they looked around and they noticed us in this shed. They approached us, they asked, "who are you?". My neighbour said that we were here from the neighbourhood and they asked, "are you from one of these two houses that are on fire?" , and she said yes. They looked at each other and they said, "the job was done there, but what do we do with them?". I was afraid for my children, that they would take them away. I looked down and I just kept silent. I did not dare even cry. One of them said, "shall we kill them or shall we go to the headquarters, to the Pican's cafe to ask what to do with them?". We kept silent and in the end they decided that they would leave us there and go to the headquarters and find out what to do, but they told us we could not leave until they came back. We kept sitting there, we waited, what our fate was going to be because we saw we were at their mercy. We could see or hear nobody from the Muslims, there was no resistance, there was no one, as if all at once everything had either died or was killed. We still waited, we heard a sound, it was a personnel carrier which was coming from the direction of Vitez. I asked my neighbour to come out so that we would be seen, so that I could take the children out of these flames, they were hungry and they already had peed and I could not change them. My son, who was only a few months old, was barefoot. It was difficult for us to wait, but we decided to come out towards these tanks so they did not notice us, because we did not dare come all the way out, because the shooting was still going on. They passed by and went to the mosque and they picked up whoever was there, and they drove them away. We stayed here, we kept waiting. After a while, a group of women came to us with a disabled small girl who was carried by them. I do not know the number, but there was quite a few of us. When they saw us, it looked as if they rejoiced because they found someone because they too have lost everybody who was male. They came to us and then we all cried. We asked who survived of whom and we saw that this is everybody who was left was there. Then we heard a second tank, the sound of it, and we decided to come out as a group so that we would be observed and that we would be taken away from all these flames, because there were flames all over, and shooting. They said that they talked to the first group of tanks and that they were told that we should stop the second group, so we decided to come closer to the road. We all went there in a group, except for my neighbour's son, he did not dare go there, so he just went past a house and the tanks approached and they noticed us. We came out and we all rushed over there and they said that we could not all get in, but we did not dare stay behind because they were our only salvation, or else we would be burned alive. They picked us up and the first tank moved on to see if there were any others around and the 16 of us came into this tank, and as we were leaving, I turned around to look at the house where my husband's body was and his life was cut short at 30. That is the last thing I remember, entering that tank. After that, I do not know anything. When we came near Travnik, I only heard from my neighbour, her son says, "mum, wake up, please look at me, I do not want to lose you as well", because they had lost father and son. He said, "mum, it is already Travnik, just come to, look around". I also came to at that point, and I saw that we had left those flames, but I carried with me the pain that I will never forget and my child will never forget it. One of them was less than 10 years old and they watched as her innocent father was being killed, who defended them in the war against the Serbs and who thought that he was safe where he was, and who was killed by those who were supposed to help in this defence. They brought us to Travnik in front of the hospital. There we were given first aid, and they offered it to those who were in need of it. After that, they drove us to where we asked to be taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Prosecutor, Witness J has visibly suffered from this, so maybe if you could just focus on a few points, maybe some exhibits might be presented, I assume you have additional questions. If you could put them in line with what we said earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I would like at first to show the witness, Witness J, Exhibit 132. It need not go on the ELMO, it is a map which is an enlargement of Exhibit 50, Defence counsel, the witness and your Honours can look at it and examine the locations, revealing the actual locations on the ELMO will, of course, identify the witness. Mr. President, there are two locations on here, number 1 and number 2, and Witness J, correct me, but the house that you were living in on the morning of 16th April is listed as number 1, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the house that you have identified as Vlado, that is Vlado Santic's house, that is number 2, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness J, you and your family were Muslims, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And Vlado Santic's house was not damaged on that day, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not by a single bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Vlado Santic is a Croat, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When your husband was murdered on the morning of 16th April, how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband was wearing a black cotton T-shirt and longjohns. When I told him the shooting had started he was only able to put on socks and that was how he was killed and that is how he remained, under the blanket.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So he was in his night clothes, the clothes that he had worn to bed that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You and your children were also in your bed clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were also in our pyjamas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your husband was home on leave from the front-line in Turbe, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And he was in the army of the BiH, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at that time. It had still not been formed. It was TO. After his death, the army was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he bring his weapon home from the front-line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not allowed to do that because the weapons were always left in the command in Travnik. We had nothing, we did not have hand grenades or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was your father-in-law living in that house with you on 16th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my father-in-law lived with us and in the morning he went out, we had an outhouse and he stayed there for a while and at that moment, the shooting started. He never came back. We still do not know where he is, he is still missing. He has not been accounted for dead or alive. We asked the Red Cross, we tried to find out something, anything, but we could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you have never seen or heard from him again after the morning of 16th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You mentioned the first group of soldiers that came to Vlado Santic's house and they had --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- camouflage uniforms on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They came after you had run across the field and you were being shot at, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you were being shot at running from your house to Vlado Santic's house, were you carrying your daughter with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I led her and my son at that time was 2 years and 2 months old and he was carried by the neighbour. When they started shooting, I just threw her to the ground and I covered her with my body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The second group of HVO soldiers, we had the first group in camouflage, the second group had camouflage uniforms and they had white belts on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did they discuss whether or not they were going to kill you and the other Muslims that were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were asking each other what to do with us, that is that second group, whether to kill us or whether to go to the headquarters in Pican's cafe to ask them what to do with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness J, was there ever an attempt by any member of the HVO to try to protect the Muslim civilians on the morning of 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were not, even though my neighbour called them by their names, she knew them, she was a native of Ahmici, but nobody responded or came to our aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you ever recover your husband's body or your father-in-law's body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never. It is painful to me when my children ask me when they will visit the grave of my husband, I do not know what to tell them, because we do not know where he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. (Pause). Mr. President, we have some identifying information concerning this particular witness and I would ask if we go into private session at this point and just identify some of these individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So we will go into a private session to protect the identifying material that you are going to have to give to the court. (In private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So now we are back in public session, but you are still subject to the same protective measures. Please counsel, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness J, the UNPROFOR tank, when you saw it picking somebody up by the mosque, when was that, what time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I did not have a watch on my wrist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But what time of day, was it in the afternoon or the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon. I just know that we saw the first tank some time around 4.00. We saw them coming because there was another group of women who caught up with us and the young son of one of my neighbours had a wrist watch, so I knew what time it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So what time was it on that watch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When they were picking people up by the mosque, did you see who got on to the tank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. The mosque is further away and I was in the shed and I did not dare go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell me, did you see your husband being killed or did you only hear the shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see the soldiers, but I saw him fall by the door, because I was standing behind the door, it was ajar and he was just standing there with his hands up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you. You told the investigators of the Tribunal earlier on that your husband belonged to the 312th Motorised Brigade of the BH-Army, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Afterwards it was formed as such. Perhaps I was a bit confused when I was speaking, because I knew the brigade that he was supposed to belong to afterwards when I was seeking aid for my children, but at the time of his life, it was the TO, the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nobilo. Now Mr. Kehoe, maybe you have some additional questions, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do not have an additional question, Mr. President, but I have been reminded by my colleague that the photograph 133/2 is a photograph of Witness J and we would like to also ensure that that is under seal, given the fact that she is a protected witness. With that note, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That is a good point. So you do not have any further questions, so Witness J, I am looking at my fellow judges, whether they have any additional questions. Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, I am sorry to call you Witness J, because I cannot say your name. When the soldiers, when the people knocked at your door in the morning, did you look from the window to see what they looked like, or did you see afterwards if they were soldiers? Did they announce themselves as soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not knock at all. They had shot a burst of gunfire because the door was locked and that is how they opened it and walked in. I did not see them. Afterwards my neighbour told me that she saw them and she saw three soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted), all the houses that I knew were Muslim houses were on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You mentioned that when you were running towards the house, what was the other house, Vlado's house, you were running in the fields with your child, you were shot at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you have any men with you, any fighting men with you running, or were you just women and children running or men without arms, and who was shooting at you? Could you explain that a little bit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I told you, my neighbour, her sister-in-law, my son, who wore my skirt over his pants, my younger child, my mother-in-law, my sister-in-law, they were the first group that was running across the field. Because my little daughter did not want to leave her father to burn, I stayed on a bit longer in front of the house where I had been staying before. They had already run across half of the field and I had not even started. They continued to run and I was only halfway when earth fell all over me, because this was a stronger detonation. I could not tell from what direction it was coming, because they were shooting from all sides. They hid behind the bushes that you can see towards Vlado's house. They told me when I could go on running. Then I continued to run, I joined them, then we all moved to Vlado's shed because that was the only place we could get into, because everything else was padlocked. We did not have a thing, we were not even dressed properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So I gather from what you said that there was shooting just at anybody who was moving, regardless of what it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everything, it did not matter who it was, small, big, young, old, male, female, they were killing everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Then when you arrived beside Vlado's house, you said that soldiers from the HVO with the insignia of the HVO, asked what to do with you and said, "why do we not kill them", and went to get instructions. Did they come back with the instructions or did they disappear after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not come back. In the meantime, the tanks started arriving, so that was our salvation and we got out. They did not come back soon after they had left. We stayed on and waited, according to their orders, but the tanks and personnel carriers started coming in and we boarded them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You heard them say that Vlado's house was not burnt because it was the house of a Croat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if it was not the house of the Croat, it would have been burnt too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably, according to what they were saying, and according to my own view, because really all Muslim houses that morning were in flames, and all the houses I knew to be Croat houses were not burning at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Witness J, I only have one little question for you. Judge Riad asked you a little while ago about the time when the second group of soldiers came, and they asked what they should do with you and your family, and I think you had said earlier on that one of them said, "shall we kill them or shall we go to the headquarters at Pican's cafe to ask what we should do with them?". All I want to know is whether you were familiar with Pican's cafe and with the headquarters at the cafe to which the speaker was referring.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know about it at all, I did not know about any kind of headquarters. Not only me but no one else, nobody had thought that something like that would happen. I hardly ever went by there, I had very young children and I had a lot to do for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you understand what kind of headquarters they were referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they said "the headquarters", I realised it was something that belonged to them, not the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There we are, Witness J, thank you very much. You said what you wanted to say. Is there anything you would care to add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if I can ask you this, but I will try: will I ever find out anything about my husband's body and my father-in-law's body and where their graves are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I can understand and my fellow judges understand your concern. It is not within the judges' powers per se to meet your concerns, but I think that as far as the Office of the Prosecution goes, through this trial and the material emerging, efforts will be made to act and all we can do is hope. We do not have any direct means, but we have heard your appeal and I think on the side of the Prosecution it has been heard and in particular by the Witness Protection Unit, that with the people to deal with, so do not hesitate, stay in touch with them, write to them and perhaps there will be some results forthcoming. Thank you very much, Witness J, now you may return home and I do hope insofar as it is possible, that you will find some peace of mind. Maybe the Registrar could ask the usher to show the witness out, but do not move for a second, madam, we are going to pull down the blinds so you may not be identified because we are in a public session. Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So we are in a public session, Mr. Cayley? Counsel, is the following witness protected? I take it he is not, because the Registrar is removing everything, so there is no protection for this next witness and you are going to tell us, just as your colleague did very briefly, what the purpose of your calling this witness is and what you want him to say. Before we bring in the witness, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, your Honours, learned counsel. The next witness is a man by the name of Colour Sergeant Andre Kujawinski. He was a platoon sergeant with the Cheshire Regiment while they were serving as a component force of the UN Protection Force in the former Yugoslavia. He served in Bosnia from November 1992 to May 1993. He was in Vitez on the morning of 16th April and was a witness to the large-scale property destruction that occurred that morning in the village -- in the town, I am sorry. On the afternoon of 16th April, he was in Ahmici, and he saw the aftermath of the attack. He observed a large number of corpses of women and children lying in open ground. He then witnessed, and in fact this will tie in with the previous witness who has just testified, a large number of women and children fleeing the village, to whom he eventually returned and rescued and took to Travnik. In fact this lady who has just testified may well be one of the individuals who he rescued and took to Travnik. He remained in the village of Ahmici that day, he witnessed again the large scale property destruction, houses were still burning. He also saw the destruction of livestock, the deliberate shooting of animals in the village. On 17th April, the witness returned to Vitez and encountered a woman who had been raped and whose husband had been shot in front of her and whose property had been stolen. Later that day, he returned to Vitez and rescued what he thought were -- what he had been led to believe were three injured Croat women, but who transpired to be three HVO soldiers, who he took to the military hospital at Nova Bila. Finally, this witness was involved in the recovery of bodies in a village called Miletici, up near the Serb front-lines, where a number of Croat men had been killed by the Mujahedin. The problem, your Honour, in presenting the evidence in the manner in which you suggested, and I have no objection to what has been suggested, I think it will speed things up tremendously, is that this was a witness who remained in the area in Bosnia, Central Bosnia, for many, many months. If he gives his testimony in a narrative form he will be speaking of a series of connected events, many of which are completely irrelevant to this trial. The events which are relevant to the trial are a number of disconnected events for which I will need to lead him in his evidence. Mr. Hayman has interviewed a number of these people and he knows, they have a lot of information which is neither relevant for the Prosecution or the Defence. I will try my best to allow the witness to speak freely, but I fear if I just allow him to talk on, we will have much evidence that has no relevance to this trial at all, but I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. That makes things clearer and as I said, we can really focus on the essentials. If I have understood rightly, what you are looking for in this witness is his testimony as to the destruction, to damage and then 17th April when he came back to Vitez and then participation in picking up the bodies, that is what you are going to be stressing, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think the points that I would stress are the property destruction in Vitez and Ahmici, a large number of bodies in Ahmici and also a point, actually, which I did not recall, the presence of a very large number of Croat soldiers just outside Ahmici on 16th April 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Okay, fine. So we are going to proceed in the same manner, we are going to do it basically the same manner. As we the judges told you, it is your witness and you can interrupt him. The account he is going to be making will be guided by you, I think that is very worthwhile, and then when he is done it will be for you to ask him for further information on points which you think are of the most importance. Needless to say, you may interrupt him, but do not interrupt him too often, because otherwise we will not speed things up at all, on the contrary. But now it is clear to me what you are looking for, the Defence also knows, so things are perfectly clear to all the parties. It has taken us three minutes, but I think these three minutes are well spent, Mr. Cayley. Let us call Sergeant Andre Kujawinski.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: One point, Mr. President, if I may ask him a few preliminary questions about his background? I do not suggest to go through his entire military history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I was going -- we have already made a lot of headway, Mr. Cayley, with this preliminary introduction. Do not forget that the Defence is watching you closely. If you ask him what he has done since elementary school, the Defence will be unhappy about that, so be very careful, only ask preliminary questions which may be relevant to our proceedings. Is that clear, so just that we focus on those questions, thank you. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Sergeant, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Before reading the solemn oath, just tell us your first and last names, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Andre Peter Kujawinski.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There is a bit of a problem, the microphone has to be turned on now. You know how these things work. Okay, please repeat your first and last names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Andre Peter Kujawinski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine, that was clear. If you please remain standing and read the solemn oath which the usher is going to give you. SERGEANT KUJAWINSKI (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Sergeant. This is customary, Sergeant, in your country, that before you sit down you remove your belt, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine, well, we keep learning something new every day. Wonderful. So the testimony is going to unfold as follows. The Prosecution, because you are a witness for the Prosecution, is going to put a few short questions to you related to identification. Then you are going to make your statement to the court. You are going to tell us about the events related to the trial of General Blaskic and this has to do with the events in April 1993 when you were stationed in the region concerned by the events and what you saw in terms of the soldiers who were there, paramilitary or military, of the HVO, also participation in collecting bodies, so I would ask you to focus in particular on those events. Counsel for the Prosecution will be leading you, will be keeping what you say focused on these main concerns and then there will be some questions and then needless to say thereafter the Defence and judges will be putting questions to you. Now for purposes of identification, please, Sergeant -- then after the identification, we will be having our recess, so Mr. Cayley, if you would like to begin with identification and then just thereafter we will have our recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. President. Sergeant Kujawinski, you remind me of a drill instructor at the Royal Military Academy at Sandhurst. What year were you born?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you joined the British army as a private soldier, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you have served in the United Kingdom, the Falkland Islands, Hong Kong, Germany, Central America and the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you are currently a colour sergeant instructing officer cadets at the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you served in the former Yugoslavia from November 1992 until May 1993, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That was when the Cheshire Regiment was part of the United Nations Protection Force in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your position at that time, was that of platoon sergeant, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who was your platoon commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Second Lieutenant Tudor Ellis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now Captain Tudor Ellis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your company commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time Major Martyn Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now Lieutenant Colonel Martyn Thomas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think there were 36 soldiers and (text currently unavailable) in that platoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was your role, what was the job of the platoon sergeant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Overall, to maintain discipline, overlook training and the day-to-day general running of the 36 men, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think the majority of your time in the former Yugoslavia was spent patrolling and performing convoy escort duties in and around Central Bosnia, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You did this in Warrior armoured personnel carriers, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you were out on the ground a lot, would that be correct to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I just have a couple of questions, Mr. President, then I will be finished. Towards the end of November, your platoon deployed to Kladanj, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your platoon returned from Kladanj to Vitez in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Later on your whole company went to Tuzla with Colonel Thomas, that was in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Then in mid January you returned to Vitez where, mid January 1993, where you remained for the rest of your service in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, those are all the preliminary questions I have for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. We will resume at 11.40. (11.20 am) (A short break) (11.40 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Court is in session. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Sergeant, you may be seated. Sergeant, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good. As we agreed with the Prosecution, you are going to make your statement to the court directly; that is to say you are going to be focusing on the three or four points which the Prosecution would like you to address in the context of these accusations against General Blaskic, the destruction, the 17th April, what you did at Vitez, then recovering the bodies, so please focus on that, but do not fear if you should forget anything, Mr. Cayley will briefly redirect you back to it and then there will be questions from Mr. Cayley and questions from the Defence. Please proceed, Sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sergeant Kujawinski, a few days before the events of 16th April, I think you had occasion to go to Travnik and then Zenica. Can you tell the court about those two journeys you made and the state in which you found Travnik and Zenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were tasked by the Ops Room to go into Travnik to show presence on the ground in the form of vehicle patrols in the Warriors. As we entered Travnik to a roadblock that was on a junction that went up to a place called Guca Gora, the roadblock that was normally there only manned by one or two soldiers was now heavily manned, with people in masks, i.e. balaclavas drawn over their faces. Because of the Summs we were getting, telling us that tension was high in the area, the form now of entering a road block was for one vehicle to enter, the other vehicle to stand off and protect that other vehicle whilst it was in the actual roadblock itself. Upon doing this, the first vehicle seemed to be there for a while, so I then took it upon myself to enter the roadblock with the second vehicle, i.e. my second vehicle, to find out what the hold-up was. The masked men demanded that they should search our vehicles and that they should check our identities. Upon not agreeing to this, only the showing of our ID cards, one of the masked men then proceeded into like a little portacabin hut which was on the left side of the road and came out with a rocket-propelled shoulder-fired launcher, and pointed it at the vehicle in terms that, I believe, saying if we do not go with what they say he is going to fire this at us. I knew this was not possible due to the range he was at, so I said he would not do it, and he then proceeded to aim the rocket-propelled grenade launcher at the drive wheel, which is a sprocket at the front of the vehicle which, if taken out, will stop the vehicle from moving. I then gestured to the man with a finger to wait while I climbed down from the turret of the vehicle, still inside the vehicle, you can do this inside the vehicle, proceeded to the back of my vehicle to take out a shoulder-fired weapon myself, which is a 94 millimetre which is used for taking tanks out and things alike. I extended the launcher, put it on my shoulder, and aimed it towards him in a gesture as he was doing, upon which he then returned to his hut and we passed through the checkpoint on to Travnik. Upon entering Travnik, we found a complete different setting to what was normal in Travnik. Houses, prior to us arriving, had been boarded up with large pieces of wood sloping away from the high-rise buildings that were there and the smaller buildings. Not many people were on the streets, if any at all. We drove up the road. On the right is the school on high ground and some cross firing was going on, just small arms fire. On the right-hand side, we saw a man who we believed to be dead on the right-hand side of the road. We went up, turned round, got around to protect him while one of the soldiers got out from the vehicle and checked that this man was in fact actually dead. He was not, he was just very drunk, so we left him there. We then continued to show a presence, which was what our task was, in Travnik and drive round the town very slowly and carefully observing what was happening, which was not a lot, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think later that day you proceeded to the city of Zenica, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe to the court briefly the atmosphere in Zenica? Again, this is a number of days before the events of 16th April 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. As mentioned, we were tasked to go to Travnik. The reason for our deployment there with all the platoon vehicles, which is five all in all, now and the OC, Major Thomas, his vehicle, was again to show a presence on the ground. Prior to leaving, we were told that a commander had been kidnapped and four of his bodyguards had been shot and our task now was to get into Zenica and show a presence on the ground again to try and calm people's feelings. Upon driving into Zenica, which is a much larger town, if not a city I suppose, compared to Travnik, the same sort of atmosphere met us. There was no one out on the ground except for soldiers with weapons. There was no civilians out, which was very unusual for Zenica, there is loads of happy people normally walking around. Again there was no signs of any boarding up or anything taking place, but the atmosphere was very still, which was very unusual, as I have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let us now move ahead to the events of 16th April, and I will put in front of you a pre-prepared exhibit. You drew certain lines with me on an aerial photograph to assist your testimony so you can represent events on the ground. If I could request that Exhibit 134 be placed in front of the witness? Normally I would ask you questions about these various locations, Colour Sergeant, but if you can just, as you narrate the events of 16th April in Vitez, refer to the aerial photograph and the areas which you marked on that photograph related to your testimony by the numbers next to the particular objects marked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead, Sergeant, you have the map before you, so if you give your account and just point to wherever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were tasked in the morning to drive down the main street of Vitez itself, which is the area marked as box 1, going all the way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Sergeant, you need but refer to the figure, this is a public session, we have these letters here so as you give your account, you have the document before you, you can say it is the main street, this is 1, with the figure 1, so just try to keep it brief with the pointer. The public sees this as well as we do, so it is perfectly clear. Go right ahead, Sergeant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So we drove down the main high street, all the way down in the area of box 1, where we saw large amounts of destruction of houses, on the left mainly, and on the right side of the road. This took the form of houses still on fire, houses smouldering away, furniture all strewn from houses and thrown about the road and the area of the houses, broken glass, curtains blowing in the wind and general destruction of the property in the forms of houses, walls and roofs all scattered about the road. As we were driving down through that area, we noticed a victim lying on the left-hand side of the road in a blue, dark blue top which I was led to believe was an old man. He was dead on the side of the road. We continued to drive down very slowly, at crawling speed, all the way down to point 3, which we commonly used as a turn-around point. We turned around and we then drove back up to the area or back through the area of Vitez. As we approached area number 2, coming back, it was unusual to note that the fact that area 2 was not as -- was not as affected as area 1 was, there were just several houses in this area destroyed in the same way as area 1. We then drove up into area 4, which we used to call the built-up area, because it was high-storey flats and that. We drove round this area in no set pattern, just checking everything. In this area here, there were no signs of destruction, there were just signs -- there were no signs of nobody out, everyone was out of the way and I refer to it as a ghost town basically, nobody there. We then drove from area 4 on to area 5 by the football stadium. As we entered that area, we drove down and stopped somewhere round by the stadium looking down the road towards point 7 where we noticed some movement on the left-hand side of the road. I stopped, or I told the vehicle to stop. We observed with the hand-held sights that we have from our weapons to notice that it was a dog of a description on the left-hand side of the road. We drove down again very cautiously and slowly, noting what was around us and when we got to point 6, we noticed a very young boy, an age of approximately 6, which I referred to as my son, because he was in that age group at the time. The puppy was alive, it was walking around him and it had come to rest every now and then in his arm. The boy was laid in an unusual way, as if he had fallen there, and as we drove a little further to look at him, we could see he had been shot in the centre of the forehead. We then continued down to point 7 just beyond the houses, which again we used to use as a common turn-around point on the grass; turned round, looked back down to area 5, drove past the body again, now on the right, back to area 5 and then reported back to the school at Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I clarify some points at this stage, or do you wish me to wait until the end of the testimony to clarify some issues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Whichever you prefer, so it is not a matter of going ahead with questioning just to come back to some points to clarify them. Briefly please, just question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Colour Sergeant, when you actually entered the town, could you hear any firing of weapons of any sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We could hear small arms fire, large amounts of small arms fire and we could hear off to the right, we believe, mortar fire of some large -- weapons being fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you actually see any weapons being fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers on that particular occasion in the town of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see any military engagement between two opposing forces in Vitez that morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think in the early afternoon of that same day you were then tasked to go to the village of Ahmici to collect or assist in the collection of an armoured personnel carrier that had broken down in the village, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Again the same procedure as before, I will present you with an exhibit which you have marked and then if you can narrate the account of events in Ahmici on that day, so if the witness could please be given Exhibit 135? Two copies again, please, one in front of him and one on the ELMO. Following the photograph, just narrate the events. If you can commence with telling the court at approximately what time you arrived in this area and from where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In the early afternoon, I was tasked from the Ops Room at the school --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can we just clarify a point? What do you mean when you say "the Ops Room"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The operations room which was the main cell for information from the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is the brain of the battalion where people are tasked, where intelligence is being gathered, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. You must book in when you arrive there and you must book out reporting any incidents that have happened en route.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We were tasked in the early afternoon to go to a grid, I was given a grid to report to, where a Scimitar vehicle, which is a smaller scale of a Warrior, had broken down along into another unit of 9th and 12th Lancers. Myself and a crew and a REME vehicle, which is basically the people that fix vehicles, proceeded down towards this grid. As we approached the area of the Zenica turnoff which went around the back way to Zenica, there is a long stretch of road going town towards a small hill. As we approached, we could see on the horizon lots and lots of smoke billowing out from an area on the left-hand side. We moved quickly down the road until we approached the area of 1. As we hit this area, we then slowed right down again to crawling speed and moved from point 1 to point 2 on the main road. As we moved through there at this slow speed, we noticed lots of houses on fire, lots of houses destroyed and smouldering and to the left of the road, lots of bodies, women and children strewn about the fields, which in a -- in a manner of which they were fleeing, i.e. they were in the open basically, they were not protected. We continued at slow speed to the right-hand side of the Catholic cemetery, we followed the road to the left and just before you hit point 3, we noticed that at point 3 on a doorstep there was a man and a child which we presumed were father and son. The father had his left arm around his son, both were dead, with a large amount of thick red blood from the father's head, and a dog was licking the blood up. We then continued, again at slow pace, down the hill towards the area of box 4. By now, my mind had switched back to what I was supposed to have been doing, which was picking up a vehicle. I got to point 4, again very slow, and I noticed to the left some movement. I told the vehicle to stop. As I looked over to the left, a woman stood up and she had her hands clasped together and she was crying and asking us to help her. I told her in actions to wait for ten minutes and that I would return to help her. I then ordered one of the soldiers to get out of the back of the vehicle, told her to stay behind the mud bank that she was by and told him to cover them up with some leaves and branches that were about the area. We then continued down the road, again at a slow pace, trying to find my bearing now, trying to find my location on the map, past point 5. As we passed it, I noticed people on the left-hand side. I continued out to point 6, which is a large turn-around area which again was commonly used, a very wide-angle berth on the river. I turned around, I told the driver to stop and as we looked back at point 5, which we commonly referred to as the Swiss chalet, I noticed a large amount of soldiers in dark uniforms in and around the chalet area. It was a large house, like an apex house, with a very huge forecourt, patio-style thing on the front. This was full of soldiers. This to date was the largest number of soldiers that I have seen together on the tour of Yugoslavia or the former Yugoslavia. I then made my way again slowly towards point 5. When I got there or as we were approaching, it was very unusual to notice that these soldiers were all commonly dressed the same, in very dark uniforms, which was unusual. Soldiers normally mixed dress, i.e. civilian tops or bottoms or vice versa, with a military top or whatever. They all had weapons and they were all drinking beer from bottles and cans. They were very happy, they were cheering, they were waving the bottles in the air towards us, gesturing towards us and the rifles and waving them in the air. At this point then, anger took over. I told the vehicle to stop, I traversed the turret of the tank towards these people and aimed the gun at them. I had done this because I basically put one and one together, the scenes that I had seen and all these so-called soldiers in this area and come up with a conclusion. I then drove off past point 4, again these people appeared behind the mud bank. I told them to stay there, then drove up the road until I came to the area marked here where I knew my grid was now to turn off to come up this road, up this track, again noticing, as I was driving down this road towards point 7, that there were again lots of houses on fire, burning and destroyed, as I was heading towards that point 7. I got to point 7, I turned my vehicle round to let the recovery vehicle pass through, because at this point now we had spotted the broken-down vehicle. He went in to assist with the fixing of this vehicle, whilst we moved forward to where the figure 7 is, the very bottom of it, to protect him whilst he done this and we looked south in this area here, whilst he carried out fixing it. The area where he was in area 7 was like houses that had not been destroyed, that were very old, they had been neglected, they were falling down, the beams were rotten et cetera, and they continued in that area for a period of time to try and fix this vehicle that had broken down. Whilst they were doing that, as I said, we gave them some protection. We then heard gunfire of some sort coming from the north here (indicates) on the high ground. We then traversed the turret again to observe where this was coming from, but we could not pinpoint the gunmen's location so we used a method taught in training, which is a crack and thump method. When the bullet travels through the air from the muzzle of the rifle it makes a crack, which gives you the direction of where the weapon is fired and then you get a thump, which is where the bullet displaces the air and that gives you where the weapon is actually firing to. We used this method and we looked in towards the area marked 8. Traversed the turret round to face that way, which is south, and we noticed several amounts of cattle strewn throughout the field which were dead, with the exception of this one that was constantly being shot, it would fall down, the rifle men would shoot again -- the cattle would get up, it would shoot again, it would fall down and this happened several time until the cattle stayed down. The vehicle was then unfixable, the REME was attached it to themselves and they towed it out. We went back then the same route as mentioned down the track, turned right past point 1 and headed off back towards the garage, first of all to drop off the broken-down vehicle with the REME, and then I reported as normal back into the school, into the Ops Room to say that I am back, and reported what I had seen and informed them that I had to go back to point 4 to pick up some people. I took another vehicle with me, went back to point 4 at speed. As we entered point 4, I stopped and loaded these people up. There now was 13 women, two children and later, just as we were closing the doors, a very young man came running from a fenced area. We took them on board, all 16 of them; even though you cannot get them into a vehicle, somehow we managed. We closed the door, we turned around. Before turning around, I looked to my rear at the other vehicle and he was doing the same movement, he had reversed back and he was now loading people on that had fled from a house on the left-hand side as we were looking back. At great speed then we moved to Travnik hospital. As we made our way back there, one of the women in the back was fainting, so we had to open the roof of the Warrior vehicle. We gave them tea and biscuits from inside the vehicle, and they were very emotional, upset, distraught, as we drove up to Travnik. Once we got there, we then entered the hospital where doctors and nurses came out to us, we opened the back of the vehicle and these people then got out of the vehicle. One of them in particular was what appeared to be a very young girl who had some sort of Down's Syndrome and disability to the fact that her legs could not close, her legs just looked like one continuous bone and she was cradled by an older woman, presumably her mother. Another woman that got out of the vehicle was a very old woman and she was very upset by this time, and she cuddled me and held on to me and she would not let go, even though the doctors were pulling her away. We both became emotional to that point. We then left them in the hospital and we then moved back towards the school to report back in, to tell them what we had done and waited to be tasked from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just a few questions to clarify a couple of matters. Mr. Usher, if you could -- you said that in the village of Ahmici when you were driving from points 1 and 2 you saw a number of bodies of women and children on the left-hand side of the road; do you recall how many bodies you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, a rough figure of 13, sir, as we were counting them, that was from point 1 to 2 and when we came back and drove up to point 7, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: These women and children were in open ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to the court, if you can recall, the women, how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were dressed in clothing that we have seen before, which is the long silk or cotton gowns with the head scarves on, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: They were dressed in normal Muslim attire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could just look at the photograph and if a copy could be placed on the ELMO, I think this is a photograph you took at the time in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now you have those three pictures before you, Sergeant, could you make a few comments on these pictures? Did you take all three of these, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only see one at the moment, sir. Yes, I did take this photograph on the first passage from point 1 to point 2 as we drove past the village. Everywhere I went I carried a camera with me and I also made a diary every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe to the court what this photograph shows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is the left-hand side of the road as we were driving from point 1 to 2 and it shows to the rear houses still burning, it shows destruction on the left and in this particular photograph it shows here and here (indicates) two bodies in the open, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you now refer to the next photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this is now once we had dropped off the broken-down vehicle at the garage, returned to the school to tell them that I had to go back to pick up some people that I had told I would be back for and the photograph, again taken by myself, is from the back of my vehicle. You just note here the antenna, taken back towards the other vehicle. We have now loaded up with the people from behind the mud bank which is here to the right (indicates) and this other vehicle is loading up with other people that have come from a house pointed out on the left-hand side. At the last minute, as I mentioned, a very young man came running from this fenced area here to get into the back of my vehicle, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar, those exhibits are 136/1 and 136/2, the two photographs. Just a couple of very brief points, Colour Sergeant. You said at the Swiss chalet that you saw a large number of soldiers drinking beer. Approximately how many did you see at the Swiss chalet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would recall it as a company sized group, sir, which in British military terms is approximately 100 men, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you notice any badges on these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I noticed on one of the left forearms a shield that was coloured red, white and blue with something above it, but I do not know what. I have no memory of that, no distinct memory, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You say these soldiers were drinking beer and toasting you, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You say that you were extremely angry. What actually prevented you from taking any action against these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Discipline, sir, good training, amongst other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You mentioned at point 7 on this photograph that there were a number of houses behind you that were dilapidated, not burnt but in fact dilapidated and left. How many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two, sir, I guess. Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Finally, the people that you transported, the villagers that were fleeing that you put in the back of your vehicle and the other vehicle, can you describe in more detail their state, how they were, how they seemed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ones we picked up from behind the mud bank?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very distraught, sir. They wanted to get away, they were -- initially when we got there, one of the women was praying, her hands clasped like so. When we actually got them into the back of the vehicle, they were trembling, they were frightened, they were distraught. Just scenes of unpleasantness, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The houses in Ahmici, were any of them fortified in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see any dead soldiers lying around on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw no dead soldier, sir. I saw one male, that was all, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: With the young child at point 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think now we can move on to the events of 17th April, and if the witness again, so that he can narrate from the photograph as he goes along, if he can be shown Exhibit 137. Colour Sergeant Kujawinski, a point of clarification, the bodies that you saw in Ahmici on your first journey through, when you returned to collect the fleeing villagers, were the bodies still there or had they gone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were still there, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like you to recall the events of 17th April, when I think you were tasked to go to Vitez to collect an UNHCR worker and his family.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you explain to the court the events of that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I was tasked now to go -- I was tasked again from the Ops Room to go into the town of Vitez, to extract an UNHCR man and his family from a given place and to withdraw them back to the school, as Vitez was now declared unsafe. We drove again down the main high street, slowly again, down towards the area marked 1, in the built-up area, where we waited and eventually they came out and we picked up a man, his wife and a child with their belongings. They got into the back of the vehicle, we closed the doors and then we drove off back to the main road here, and then continued down the main road, commonly again to the turn-around point, turned around and made our way back up the main road until we hit point 2. As we approached point 2, a very frightened woman ran out from a house. We opened the back doors, she got in, we closed the doors and through the UNHCR man who interpreted, found out that in the last two hours she had been raped twice, money and valuables had been stolen from her and a man had been shot in front of her. We asked if she wanted to come with us to the school; unusually, she said no. I asked her to depart the vehicle, we opened the doors and she went and went back into the house. We then closed the doors and continued back towards the school following the main route and back into the school, dropping off the UNHCR man and his family and reporting back in.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit 136/3, I think that morning you actually passed by the Hotel Vitez, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Although I realise this photograph was not taken on 17th April, you made certain observations on that morning outside the Hotel Vitez and, using this photograph as a reference point and a guide to demonstrate to the court what was happening, can you explain to the court the observations that you made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again there is the photograph taken by myself looking now low down through the vehicle, looking towards the garage way, so on the left here (indicates) is the Hotel Vitez on the top, but to the right here and moreover further to the right by the sides of houses and in and around the houses, the soldiers now had dug-in positions, dug holes to stay protected behind, and built up with sand bags to give themselves protection. As we drove past that morning, we noticed a somewhat unusual but organised changeover between the actual soldiers themselves, i.e. handing over a duty from one man to another. We noted he was handing over because he was pointing out things on the ground -- appeared to be pointing out things on the ground, talking to him and then one would leave while the other one stayed there. Again unusual of this to a degree is that everyone had a weapon, they actually kept their weapon with them and moved back and to from this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How large was this group of soldiers that you saw outside the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would equivalent this to a section size, which is eight men, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Which is pretty small on the military scale of things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: They were behaving in a normal disciplined manner, in the manner you would observe as a British soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as professional sir, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But they were acting in an organised manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did they look as if they were under attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: They were just milling around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, a normal routine, as I would call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. One point of clarification. The woman who told you that she had been raped, her money had been stolen, a man had been shot in front of her, how was she dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the same way as previously mentioned, sir, this Muslim attire, this long silk or cotton gown with a shawl over her head, I think it was a woollen hat or a head-dress over this, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there any shooting in Vitez that day, was there any mortar firing or shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That day, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, on the 17th when you went to collect the UNHCR worker?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I can recall when we went to collect the UNHCR worker, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can now move on. If Exhibit 137 could be placed on the ELMO, please? Just to refresh your memory, I think on that afternoon you were requested to pick up three wounded women in the centre of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to the court, again using the aerial photograph as an indicator of the journey that you made through the town, about those events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I was now tasked again from the Ops Room to drive into Vitez and pick up three wounded women from the hospital. I previously knew this building anyway after doing many journeys through there, but before I left the Ops Room, I clarified that it was still the same hospital, i.e. it had not moved. It was, I went into the village on the normal route down the main road, I then turned off and proceeded to the area of box 3. I got there, nobody came out, which was not unusual at this time, because round by the area of the sports pitch there was some sort of battle going on, small arms fire and mortar fire ringing out. I then ordered the driver to rev the engine nice and loud and beep his horn. Prior to that, sorry, we moved into the box and we broke down a small wall so we could get as close to the building as possible. As I mentioned, then he revved his engine as loud as he could and beeped his horn, but nobody came out. I then got on the radio to the Ops Room and asked them to confirm the grid of where the hospital was at. They gave me the grid, it was the right grid, I confirmed it by looking at the satellite navigation equipment on the vehicle, which pinpoints your position. I was there. I then informed the Ops Room that nobody was at this grid. They told me to come back, pick up an interpreter and make sure that I have got the right location. So I went back to the Ops Room, as told, picked up the interpreter, moved back towards box 3. However, as I was moving there I asked the interpreter to guide us in, i.e. give us directions left, right, by her looking out of a very small window at the back. Lo and behold, we got back to box 3, which is the right location, she did confirm that this was the hospital, and again we did exactly the same, revved the engine and beeped the horn, but nothing happened. I took a decision then that we would get out of the vehicle and we would check the building to make sure that there was nobody inside the building. Myself, along with two other rifle men, Halt and Trainer, I gave them a quick brief, we exited the vehicle, we cocked our rifles to make them ready and we then went through the building checking each room to make sure that it was the right building and to see if anybody was in there. Upon the entrance to the second room of the building, we found on the floor a very old man and a very old woman who I believe had not been killed there, they had been brought there, the reason being they were laid to attention, rigid with their arms by their sides. They had been shot straight in the middle of the forehead, the pair of them, and there was no blood or nothing on the floor. The woman was dressed in the same attire, the Muslim-style clothing, as we had previously seen. I then went out of the building, after looking in a couple more rooms to find nothing, but to confirm that the hospital was not there, back to the vehicle, told the Ops Room what I had seen. I then climbed back into the turret of the vehicle, looked around and when I looked right down the road towards the area marked 4, I could see an old white Peugeot with a red cross on it -- sorry, Citroen. I then presumed that was the ambulance and a medical centre.
